title: Spaghetti Aglio e Olio: The 20-Minute Italian Classic Every Home Cook Needs
excerpt: With just garlic, olive oil, chili flakes, and spaghetti, this Neapolitan staple delivers outsized flavor from a handful of pantry ingredients — and it's naturally vegetarian.
body:
Few pasta dishes punch above their weight like spaghetti aglio e olio. The name translates literally from Italian to "garlic and oil," and the recipe holds nothing back — what you see is what you get. Originating in Naples in southern Italy, this is the kind of dish Italian home cooks have thrown together after late nights and bare-cupboard moments for generations. Now, as pasta steadily becomes a pantry staple in Indian kitchens from Mumbai to Chicago, aglio e olio is having a quiet moment among diaspora home cooks who want something fast, flavorful, and free of heavy cream sauces.

Five Ingredients, No Shortcuts

The ingredient list is short enough to memorize: 250 grams of spaghetti, six tablespoons of extra virgin olive oil, two teaspoons of finely chopped garlic, one teaspoon of red chili flakes, three tablespoons of fresh parsley, and salt. That's it. There's no onion, no tomato, no cheese in the traditional version.

The simplicity is the point — and the challenge. "With just a handful of ingredients, there is nothing to hide behind, so the way you cook each ingredient makes all the difference," writes Dassana Amit, the food writer behind Veg Recipes of India, in her recently updated guide to the dish.

"After making this Aglio e Olio pasta many times, I found that the best texture comes from finishing the spaghetti in the pan with some reserved pasta water instead of simply tossing it with garlic-infused olive oil."

— Dassana Amit, Veg Recipes of India

That reserved pasta water — starchy from cooking the spaghetti — is the unsung ingredient. When simmered with the garlic-chili oil for two to three minutes, it emulsifies into a light, glossy sauce that coats each strand without leaving the dish oily. It's a technique professional Italian chefs rely on, and it makes the difference between a mediocre aglio e olio and a good one.

The Method, Step by Step

Boil the spaghetti in generously salted water, but pull it out two to three minutes before the package time — it finishes cooking in the pan. While the pasta boils, warm the olive oil over low heat in a frying pan, add the garlic, and cook gently until it turns light golden. Burnt garlic is the single biggest mistake here; it turns the whole dish bitter.

Once the garlic is golden, kill the heat and add the chili flakes — the residual warmth is enough to bloom their flavor without scorching them. Add half a cup of the reserved pasta water, return to low heat, and let it simmer for a couple of minutes. Toss in the drained spaghetti and two tablespoons of parsley, and cook on medium-low heat, tossing constantly, until the liquid reduces into a silky coating. Finish with the remaining parsley and a crack of black pepper.

Why It Works in Indian Kitchens

Aglio e olio's appeal to Indian cooks isn't accidental. Garlic and dried red chilies are foundational to Indian cooking — tadka, the hot-oil tempering technique used across South Asian cuisines, operates on essentially the same principle of blooming aromatics in fat. The leap from a garlic-chili tadka to a garlic-chili olive oil isn't a stretch. It's almost familiar.

The dish is also naturally vegetarian and vegan, which matters in a country where an estimated 30 to 40 percent of the population follows a vegetarian diet. Unlike carbonara or bolognese, there's no egg or meat to navigate around. Indian food bloggers on platforms like Tarla Dalal and Masala Chilli have long published their own spins, sometimes adding a pinch of garam masala or substituting curry leaves for parsley.

India's broader romance with pasta is accelerating. The country's pasta market crossed $1 billion in 2024 and is projected to hit $4.3 billion by 2034, according to market research firm IMARC Group, driven largely by younger urban consumers and the explosion of quick-service restaurants. Fusion dishes — tandoori pasta, masala penne, butter chicken spaghetti — dominate restaurant menus. But at home, simpler preparations like aglio e olio are gaining ground precisely because they don't require specialty ingredients or elaborate preparation.

Tips for Getting It Right

Quality matters more here than in almost any other pasta dish. Use the best extra virgin olive oil you can afford — it's doing the heavy lifting on flavor. Fresh garlic is non-negotiable; jarred minced garlic won't deliver the same mellow sweetness when cooked low and slow. Flat-leaf parsley is the traditional choice, though curly parsley works in a pinch.

On the chili front, Indian cooks comfortable with higher heat levels can push beyond the standard one teaspoon of red pepper flakes. Some bloggers recommend sautéing thinly sliced fresh red or green chilies alongside the garlic for a sharper bite. The dish is forgiving enough to accommodate the adjustment without losing its character.

Leftovers keep in the refrigerator for a day but lose their silkiness. Reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water or olive oil rather than microwaving, which dries out the strands.

A Weeknight Standard

Spaghetti aglio e olio won't win any awards for complexity, and that's precisely the point. For diaspora home cooks juggling long workdays and the perennial question of what to make for dinner, a dish that goes from pantry to plate in 20 minutes — with ingredients most Indian kitchens already have on hand — is hard to beat. It's proof that the best cooking often comes from knowing when to stop adding things and let a few good ingredients speak for themselves.
